title: Dielectrics, Piezoelectrics and Ferroelectrics
description: Eight qualitative questions covering polarization, capacitive behaviour, dielectric loss, breakdown, piezoelectricity and ferroelectricity. Multiple-response items use +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero. Includes interfacial polarization, loss-current phase, breakdown mechanisms and ferroelectric properties from Dielectric w Piezo.

questions.prompt: What happens when an ideal dielectric is polarized by an applied electric field?

options.content: A net dipole moment per unit volume can develop.
A steady flow of free carriers through the bulk is required for polarization.
Positive and negative bound charges shift slightly relative to one another.
Bound polarization charge can appear at surfaces.

questions.explanation: Polarization is the displacement or alignment of bound charge, producing electric dipoles and possibly bound surface charge. It does not require the continuous free-carrier transport that defines conduction current.

questions.prompt: Match the qualitative polarization mechanisms to physical motion. Which statements are correct?

options.content: Electronic polarization occurs only in molecules that already have permanent dipoles.
Electronic polarization displaces an electron cloud relative to its nucleus.
Ionic polarization shifts positive and negative ion sublattices relative to each other.
Orientational polarization aligns permanent molecular dipoles.

questions.explanation: Electronic polarization can occur in every atom because the electron cloud can distort. Ionic polarization involves relative ion displacement, while orientational polarization requires permanent dipoles that rotate toward the field.

questions.prompt: A heterogeneous insulating sample contains regions with different conductivities. Mobile charges collect at internal interfaces but cannot pass freely across them. Which statements correctly identify the mechanism?

options.content: Material heterogeneity can make this mechanism important.
It requires every molecule to have a permanent dipole.
This is interfacial or space-charge polarization.
It means charge flows uniformly through the sample without accumulating anywhere.
It is identical to distortion of an individual atomic electron cloud.

questions.explanation: Charge accumulation at interfaces creates a macroscopic dipole contribution. It differs from electronic cloud distortion, relative ionic displacement, and rotation of permanent dipoles. Blocking interfaces are central; a spatially uniform current with no charge accumulation is not this mechanism.

questions.prompt: What is the most direct physical meaning of dielectric loss in an AC field?

options.content: All supplied energy is stored and returned with no phase lag.
Polarization lags the field, so some electrical energy is dissipated as heat.
The internal electric field is exactly zero at all times.
Only the current component exactly 90 degrees ahead of the voltage produces average heating.

questions.explanation: Polarization lags the applied electric field. Current is the time derivative of polarization, so its dissipative component is IN PHASE with the voltage, not 90 degrees out of phase. In $Y=G_p+j\omega C'$, $G_pV$ causes average heating, while $j\omega C'V$ is the quadrature, energy-storage current. Ideal capacitive current alone has zero cycle-averaged power.

questions.prompt: Which statements about dielectric breakdown are correct?

options.content: Defects, moisture and electrical aging can reduce practical breakdown strength.
Local heating can increase conduction and create destructive positive feedback.
Breakdown occurs when the electric field exceeds a material- and condition-dependent strength.
Breakdown is always perfectly reversible once the voltage is removed.

questions.explanation: Breakdown strength depends on the material, geometry, temperature, defects and history. Thermal runaway and field-enhanced carrier processes can cause irreversible damage, so removal of voltage does not guarantee recovery.

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish the direct and converse piezoelectric effects?

options.content: The direct effect converts applied mechanical stress into electrical charge.
The two effects support sensor and actuator applications, respectively.
Every centrosymmetric crystal must be piezoelectric.
The converse effect converts an applied electric field into mechanical strain.

questions.explanation: Mechanical stress can produce charge in the direct effect, while an electric field can produce deformation in the converse effect. Piezoelectricity requires suitable non-centrosymmetric structure; centrosymmetry prevents a linear piezoelectric response.

questions.prompt: Which properties are characteristic of a ferroelectric material below its Curie temperature?

options.content: It can possess spontaneous polarization without an applied field.
Its ferroelectric crystal phase permits a piezoelectric response.
An applied field can switch the polarization direction.
A ferroelectric can never show piezoelectric behaviour.

questions.explanation: A ferroelectric phase has spontaneous polarization that can be reoriented by a suitable field. The polar ferroelectric phase is piezoelectric; the converse classification does not hold, because not every piezoelectric is ferroelectric. Random domain orientations can cancel the macroscopic response of an unpoled ceramic.

questions.prompt: An isolated parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its source. Filling its gap with a linear dielectric increases both its capacitance and the voltage across its plates.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The isolated plates retain the same free charge Q. Filling the gap increases $C$ and reduces $V=Q/C$ (neglect fringing). A capacitor connected to an ideal voltage source instead maintains V and draws extra charge. These two electrical boundary conditions must not be confused.
